title: Anatomy of a Feature Page
takeaway: A labelled tour of one page of the paper's published feature browser, which puts four kinds of evidence about a single learned feature side by side: where it fires, what it does to the next-token logits, whether any single neuron matches it, and whether a parallel training run found the same thing. For the feature shown, no neuron correlates with it above 0.09, while a feature from the parallel run correlates at 0.75.
walkthrough:
This is one page from the [[feature-exploration-interface|feature exploration interface]], the published tool that has a page like this for every [[feature|feature]] in every dictionary learning run. Everything outside the grey box is annotation added for the paper. The tool itself prints none of it.

Read the page in four columns.

**Identity.** The header gives the feature's index within its run, `#3923`, and a human-written label, `Latin: ?`, whose question mark records that the labeller was not confident. Below sits an [[automated-interpretability|automated]] explanation, written by Claude from activating examples alone, and a score of $0.305$. That score is the rank correlation between the activations Claude later predicted from that explanation and the true ones.

Three tables follow. NEURON ALIGNMENT writes the [[feature-direction|feature direction]] out in the [[neuron-basis-coefficients|basis of the 512 MLP neurons]] and lists the three largest coefficients. CORRELATED NEURONS instead ranks neurons by how closely their activations track the feature's across the dataset, which is the paper's preferred way of hunting for a [[most-correlated-neuron|neuron counterpart]]. CORRELATED B FEATURES runs the same comparison against the parallel run on the second transformer, the paper's measure of [[universality|universality]] by [[activation-similarity|activation similarity]].

**Statistics.** The upper histogram counts nonzero activations by size, and its header reports [[feature-density|feature density]] — the fraction of all tokens on which this feature fires at all. Beneath it are the ten most negative and ten most positive [[logit-weight|logit weights]], the linear estimate of how firing shifts each next-token logit, with the whole distribution plotted below.

**Examples.** The third column holds the [[top-dataset-examples|top 20 activating examples]]. The fourth holds subsample intervals: [[activation-interval|evenly spaced bands]] stepping down from the maximum, so a reader can check whether the story still holds at weaker activations. In every snippet the bold token is the selected one, four tokens of context sit on each side, orange shading is activation strength, and the underline colour reports a [[feature-ablation|feature ablation]] — blue where deleting the feature raised the model's loss on that token, red where it lowered it.

**What it shows.** The layout is the paper's per-feature argument in one screen. Here the two neuron tables stay near zero while the parallel-run feature reaches 0.75, which is the shape of evidence the paper wants: not a neuron, but not a fluke either.

terms.definition: The index of this feature within its dictionary learning run, printed as a clickable link so a page can be cited by URL. Under the paper's naming scheme a full name would also carry the transformer letter and run number, as in A/1/3923.
A free-text label written by one of the paper's authors after looking at the page. The trailing question mark is the labeller flagging that the reading is tentative, not a fixed part of the format.
The automated interpretability panel: an explanation of the feature generated by Claude from activating examples alone, with no access to the human label.

How well that generated explanation predicts unseen activations. Claude is given the explanation and fresh token sequences, predicts an activation for each token, and the score is the correlation between predicted and true values.

terms.term: "The neuron attends to common Latin words and short phrases."
terms.definition: The text Claude produced for this feature. It says "neuron" because the same prompt is used for real MLP neurons and for autoencoder features, so the wording is generic rather than a claim that this feature is a neuron.

A table decomposing the feature's direction into the 512 MLP neurons and showing the three neurons with the largest coefficients. It answers whether dictionary learning simply handed back one neuron under a new name.
Which MLP neuron the row refers to, numbered within the transformer's 512-unit hidden layer. Clicking it opens that neuron's own page in the same interface.
The feature direction's coefficient on that neuron. The decoder columns are constrained to unit length, so this is a component of a unit vector and can be signed either way.

That coefficient's share of the total absolute mass of the direction, that is |value| divided by the sum of |coefficient| over all 512 neurons. The paper does not define the column in text, but the printed numbers are consistent with this reading. It is a spread-out-ness gauge: a one-neuron feature would read near 100%.

A table ranking MLP neurons by how well their activations track this feature's across a large sample of dataset tokens. The paper says it trusts this more than neuron alignment for finding a neuron counterpart, because neurons differ in activation scale.
The ordinary linear correlation between the feature's activation vector over sampled tokens and the neuron's (or the other feature's), after subtracting each one's mean.

The same comparison without mean-subtraction: the cosine of the angle between the two activation vectors. Because activations are non-negative and mostly zero, it usually lands close to the Pearson value, which is what the printed columns show.

The same activation comparison, but against features from the matched dictionary trained on the second transformer. Both transformers use identical hyperparameters and data and differ only in random seed, so a high value means two independent runs found the same thing.
The second one-layer transformer and the dictionary learned on it. The paper keeps it aside specifically to test whether features recur across seeds.

A histogram of this feature's activation values, built by sampling tokens at random and keeping only those where the feature is nonzero. Zeros are excluded, so the plot describes the shape of firing, not how often it fires.

The fraction of all sampled tokens on which the feature has a nonzero activation. The paper uses the distribution of this quantity across features as a quick proxy for whether an autoencoder trained well.
The scalar output of the feature on a token, the coefficient the autoencoder assigns to this dictionary direction. It is non-negative because the encoder ends in a ReLU.

The ten vocabulary tokens the feature pushes down hardest and the ten it pushes up hardest, by logit weight. Logit weight is computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

The logit weight value, plotted over the whole vocabulary. Softmax is shift-invariant, so there is no absolute zero; the paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero, and the listed tokens are the tails of this distribution.

The 20 dataset snippets on which this feature fires most strongly, the standard first look at what a unit responds to. The paper notes elsewhere that judging a unit only from its maximal examples flatters it.
The largest activation among the examples shown in that panel. In the top panel it is the feature's maximum over the sampled corpus; in each subsample interval it marks the top of that band.

One band of the activation range, with examples drawn from it at random. Interval 0 sits just below the top activations and the numbering counts downward, so higher-numbered intervals show progressively weaker firings.
The feature's activation on that token, with darker orange meaning a larger value. It marks where the feature fired.

The token that caused this snippet to be selected for display, that is the one whose activation placed it in this panel or interval. Everything around it is context, not part of the selection criterion.

Ablating the feature raised the model's loss on predicting that token, so the feature was helping that prediction. Ablation means recomputing the forward pass with this feature's contribution subtracted out of the MLP activations.
Ablating the feature lowered the loss on that token, so the feature was hurting that prediction. In the paper's Arabic case study this happens mostly on punctuation shared with other scripts.
A flag that this exact snippet has already been shown in another interval on the same page. It exists so a reader does not mistake a duplicate for independent evidence.
Holding the cursor on any token for two or more seconds reveals its numeric activation and ablation effect, since the shading and underline colour only encode these approximately.

terms.term: Latin-ending tokens (ibus, orem, ips, aliqu, ea, imus, orum, ulum, itor, nostr)
terms.definition: The top positive logit tokens. They are word fragments from pseudo-Latin filler text, several of them genuine Latin case and verb endings, which matches the lorem-ipsum boilerplate visible in the example snippets.

terms.term: English sports and place tokens (Rangers, Center, NBA, CW, WF, League, watch, Hockey, West, sville)
terms.definition: The top negative logit tokens: the things the feature makes less likely when it fires. They read as ordinary English proper-noun and sports vocabulary, the opposite of pseudo-Latin filler.

numbers.meaning: The feature's index inside its dictionary learning run. The run being shown is A/1, which has 4,096 features, so indices run from 0 to 4,095 and this one sits near the top of that range purely by ordering, not by importance.

The autointerp score: the correlation between the activations Claude predicted from its own written explanation and the true activations, over sixty nine-token examples. The paper reports Spearman rank correlation as its main scoring throughout, so this is a middling result, well above zero but far from a clean match.

The feature's density: it is nonzero on about 1.44 tokens in a thousand. That places it in what the paper calls the high density cluster, whose right-hand mode sits around one in a hundred thousand to one in a thousand, and well clear of the ultralow density cluster around one in ten million that the paper treats as a training artifact and excludes.

The top row of NEURON ALIGNMENT: MLP neuron 138 carries a coefficient of +0.40 in the feature's direction, which is 3.6% of the direction's total absolute mass. Neuron indices run 0 to 511 because the transformer's inner MLP dimension is 512.

The second and third alignment rows. Both print +0.27 yet differ in the percentage column, which means the underlying values differ in a decimal place the display rounds away (roughly 0.274 versus 0.269).

The implied L1 norm of the feature direction, recoverable from the table: 0.40 divided by 0.036 gives about 11.1, and 0.27 divided by 11.1 gives 2.4%, so the column is internally consistent. This is the number that makes the non-alignment argument. A direction sitting entirely on one neuron would have L1 of 1; a unit vector spread evenly over all 512 neurons would have L1 of about 22.6. At 11.1, this feature is spread across dozens of neurons, closer to the even case than to the single-neuron case.

The single most correlated MLP neuron. A Pearson correlation of 0.09 is very weak: no neuron in the layer fires in anything like the same pattern as this feature. This is the number that would have to be large for the feature to be a relabelled neuron.

The second and third most correlated neurons, weaker still. Neuron 138 is worth noticing: it is the largest single contributor to the feature's direction, yet its activations correlate with the feature's at only 0.05, which is exactly why the paper prefers the correlation table over the alignment table when checking for a neuron counterpart.

The closest feature in the parallel B run, correlating at 0.75. Across all of A/1 the median correlation with the best-matching B feature is 0.72, so this feature is a typical case of the paper's universality result. The comparable median for the closest matching neuron between the two transformers is 0.46.
The next two B-run features. The sharp fall from 0.75 to 0.10 means the match is a single specific counterpart rather than a diffuse cluster of similar features.

Counts of sampled nonzero activations per bin. The leftmost bin is the tallest at about 250, so most firings are weak; the paper's activation interval analysis exists precisely because weak firings are where interpretations tend to break down.
The activation range, ticked at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. It runs just past the observed maximum of 11.54.
The ten negative logit weights, from Rangers at −0.37 to sville at −0.29. The narrow spread means no single token is strongly suppressed; suppression is broad and shallow.

The ten positive logit weights, from ibus at +0.48 to nostr at +0.36. The positive tail is slightly larger in magnitude than the negative tail, consistent with the feature pushing toward a specific vocabulary rather than away from one.

The plotted range of logit weights over the vocabulary. The bulk sits in a single mode at zero because the weights are shifted so that each feature's median is zero; the listed tokens are the thin tails.
The largest activation seen anywhere in the sampled corpus, reported at the head of the TOP ACTIVATIONS column. All interval boundaries are fractions of this number.

The maximum activations inside subsample intervals 0, 1 and 2. The steps between them are about 0.87 and 0.83, so bands are close to evenly spaced. Extrapolating that step down to zero implies roughly a dozen bands, which fits the appendix's mention of a top-activations panel plus twelve further intervals but sits awkwardly with the callout's stated ten. The paper's own counts of intervals are not consistent across sections.
The number of top activating examples shown. Elsewhere the paper uses the same count when searching neurons for a given behaviour, so the two displays are comparable.
Rows in each of the three comparison tables. Only the top three neurons or features are listed, which is enough to show whether a match exists but not enough to characterise the full distribution.
The number of logit weights shown on each side, and the number of subsample intervals the callout names.
Tokens of context displayed on each side of the selected token, giving nine tokens per snippet. The same nine-token window is what Claude is scored on in the automated evaluation.
The hover dwell time before the tooltip with exact activation and ablation numbers appears, long enough that it does not fire while a reader is scanning.
Tokens in the subset used to build these visualizations, with only 10 tokens taken from each context so that the examples are not clustered inside a few documents.
Dataset examples used when computing the feature-to-neuron activation correlations reported in the CORRELATED NEURONS table.

The transformer's inner MLP dimension and the number of learned features in the A/1 run. The dictionary is eight times overcomplete, which is what makes it possible for a feature to have no neuron counterpart at all.
